competitor.role: Maps every coffee shop in NYC, separates chains from independents and finds under-served areas.
competitor.summary: New York City hosts 3,252 coffee shops, and about a third of them (1,112) belong to chains, with Dunkin and Starbucks accounting for the two largest footprints. The market is heavily concentrated in areas like Hell’s Kitchen, where each shop serves roughly 275 weekday subway riders, making it the most crowded neighborhood for coffee vendors. By contrast, Elmhurst in Queens is the most under‑served, with an average of 5,096 weekday riders per coffee shop, indicating a clear opportunity for new entrants.

operations.role: Studies what successful cafés do right and what gets cafés in trouble (health grades, closures).
operations.summary: Well‑run cafés tend to keep their health‑grade scores high—about 95 % of all NYC coffee shops earn an A, and the rate is even higher for chains (98 %) than for independents (94 %). The cafés that get shut down are usually those with serious sanitation lapses, especially surfaces that aren’t cleaned and sanitised properly, a problem identified at 1,869 locations. When an inspection does lead to a closure, two‑thirds of the time it’s because of pest‑related issues such as mice, roaches, flies or gaps that let pests in.

top_violations.description: Food contact surface not properly washed, rinsed and sanitized after each use and following any activity when contamination may have occurred.
top_violations.tip: Surfaces not cleaned and sanitised properly: sanitise after every use.

top_violations.description: Food not protected from potential source of contamination during storage, preparation, transportation, display or service.
top_violations.tip: Food not protected: cover food, use sneeze guards, label containers.

top_violations.description: Cold TCS food item held above 41 °F; smoked or processed fish held above 38 °F; intact raw eggs held above 45 °F; or reduced oxygen packaged (ROP) TCS foods held above required temperatures except during active necessary preparation.
top_violations.tip: Cold food too warm: keep milk and cold items at 41°F or below; check fridges daily.

top_violations.description: Filth flies or food/refuse/sewage associated with (FRSA) flies or other nuisance pests  in  establishment’s food and/or non-food areas. FRSA flies include house flies, blow flies, bottle flies, flesh flies, drain flies, Phorid flies and fruit flies.
top_violations.tip: Flies: screens, closed bins, clean drains.

top_violations.description: Evidence of mice or live mice in establishment's food or non-food areas.
top_violations.tip: Mice: seal gaps, store food off the floor, use a licensed pest-control service.

top_violations.description: Food Protection Certificate (FPC) not held by manager or supervisor of food operations.
top_violations.tip: No Food Protection Certificate holder on duty: make sure a certified manager is always on shift.

top_violations.description: Wiping cloths not stored clean and dry, or in a sanitizing solution, between uses.
top_violations.tip: Wiping cloths left out: keep them in sanitising solution between uses.

top_violations.description: Hot TCS food item not held at or above 140 °F.
top_violations.tip: Hot food not hot enough: hold hot food at 140°F or above.

lessons.title: Keep an A grade from day one
lessons.text: 95% of coffee shops have an A. Customers see the grade in the window, so a B or C puts you behind most competitors.

lessons.title: Pests are the top reason cafés get shut
lessons.text: 66% of the coffee shops the Health Department closed had a pest problem at that inspection. A pest-control contract and sealing gaps around pipes and doors are must-haves.

lessons.title: Chains run tight processes; independents can too
lessons.text: Chains hold A grades 98% of the time vs 94% for independents. Daily checklists (fridge temperatures, cleaning, pest checks) close that gap.

lessons.title: Don't open where it's already crowded
lessons.text: Areas with few riders per café split the same customers many ways. Look for busy streets that have few cafés (see the map).

picks.name: Downtown Brooklyn-DUMBO-Boerum Hill
picks.why: Downtown Brooklyn‑DUMBO‑Boerum Hill already supports a thriving café scene, with 53 coffee shops (including well‑known chains like Starbucks, Dunkin and Devocion) and a steady flow of about 2,064 weekday subway riders per shop, thanks to 111,457 daily subway entries across eight nearby stations. The area’s 800 storefronts—only 43 of which are vacant—mean you’ll have plenty of location options, and the median resident income of roughly $44,300 gives you a solid base of spending power. Recent growth (14 new coffee shops in the past two years) and an overall neighborhood score of 79/100 highlight both strong foot traffic and a supportive market for new cafés. One thing to watch: because the neighborhood is a work‑area hub, business peaks during weekday mornings to late afternoons and can dip noticeably on weekends, so plan staffing and inventory accordingly.

trace.content: New study: where should a first-time owner open a coffee shop in NYC? Each of you, report on the whole city first.
Citywide report, please.

New York City hosts 3,252 coffee shops, and about a third of them (1,112) belong to chains, with Dunkin and Starbucks accounting for the two largest footprints. The market is heavily concentrated in areas like Hell’s Kitchen, where each shop serves roughly 275 weekday subway riders, making it the most crowded neighborhood for coffee vendors. By contrast, Elmhurst in Queens is the most under‑served, with an average of 5,096 weekday riders per coffee shop, indicating a clear opportunity for new entrants.
Citywide report, please.

In the past two years, New York City saw 783 new coffee shops open, and the overwhelming majority—84%—are independent cafés rather than chain locations. The biggest concentration of these openings is in Midtown‑Times Square, where 43 new shops have launched, making it the hottest neighborhood for coffee‑shop growth. Among chains, Dunkin leads the pack with 51 new stores, followed by Starbucks (16), Cotti Coffee (7), Matto Espresso (6) and Luckin Coffee (6).
Citywide report, please.

Midtown‑Times Square is the city’s busiest commercial hub, seeing about 414,005 subway entries on an average weekday. It also has the most empty storefronts of any area, with 181 of its 2,744 spaces currently vacant. This combination of heavy foot traffic and available units makes Midtown‑Times Square a promising spot to consider for a new coffee shop.
Citywide report, please.

Well‑run cafés tend to keep their health‑grade scores high—about 95 % of all NYC coffee shops earn an A, and the rate is even higher for chains (98 %) than for independents (94 %). The cafés that get shut down are usually those with serious sanitation lapses, especially surfaces that aren’t cleaned and sanitised properly, a problem identified at 1,869 locations. When an inspection does lead to a closure, two‑thirds of the time it’s because of pest‑related issues such as mice, roaches, flies or gaps that let pests in.
